docs.title: pgfs — PostgreSQL-Backed FUSE Filesystem
docs.text:
Welcome to the pgfs documentation site, structured according to the Diátaxis framework.

pgfs is a high-performance, POSIX-compliant FUSE filesystem backed natively by a PostgreSQL database engine.

docs.title: 🧭 Documentation Structure
docs.text:
The documentation is organized across four distinct quadrants:

- :material-school: **Tutorials** --- Learning-oriented step-by-step guides to get hands-on experience with `pgfs`. docs.title: Explanation: Atomic Renames & Lock-Move Semantics
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.AtomicRename

Users can rename (move) files and directories with standard mv semantics, including overwriting existing files and empty directories.

AtomicRename guarantees POSIX compliance by wrapping entry updates and subtree path re-keying within a single PostgreSQL transaction (BEGIN ... COMMIT). This ensures no intermediate state is exposed to concurrent readers, preventing file corruption during rename-overwrite operations.

docs.title: Explanation: Dual-Interface Storage Architecture
docs.text:
Feature: spec.optimize.DualInterfaceArchitecture

pgfs features a Dual-Interface Storage Architecture providing a sub-100µs Local In-Process Engine (pgrx + zero SQL parsing + io_uring zero copy) and a scalable Remote Async Network Engine (tokio-postgres + pipelining).

DualInterfaceArchitecture decouples FUSE filesystem request dispatching from storage engine execution. The Local Engine embeds processing directly inside PostgreSQL as a background worker, bypassing SQL parsing and socket serialization for sub-100µs latency. The Remote Engine provides standard out-of-process networking using async Rust (tokio-postgres), allowing pgfs to scale seamlessly across network hosts.

docs.title: Explanation: POSIX Flat Filesystem
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.FlatFilesystem

Users can create, read, write, and delete files through standard POSIX file operations on the mounted directory.

FlatFilesystem translates POSIX file I/O operations into relational database operations on PostgreSQL. File metadata and byte payloads are mapped to database records. Reads and writes interact with stored byte arrays while presenting a standard POSIX filesystem interface to applications through FUSE.

docs.title: Explanation: Hierarchical Directory Trees
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.HierarchicalDirectories

Users can create nested directories, list their contents, and remove empty directories through standard POSIX directory operations.

HierarchicalDirectories models a directory tree within PostgreSQL using parent inode pointers (parent_ino, name) indexed by B-Tree structures. Directory traversals check parent relationships, enabling efficient hierarchy navigation while enforcing strict POSIX directory semantics.

docs.title: Explanation: Database-Native Kernel Acceleration
docs.text:
Feature: spec.offload.KernelOffloadingAcceleration

pgfs incorporates Database-Native Kernel Offloading capabilities, utilizing copy_file_range, fallocate, reflink CoW, and server-side search to eliminate userspace byte streaming and deliver sub-millisecond execution for large-scale file operations.

KernelOffloadingAcceleration moves file manipulation operations into PostgreSQL's query engine. Instead of reading bytes from disk into FUSE daemon memory and writing them back over socket buffers, pgfs intercepts Linux VFS acceleration callbacks (copy_file_range, fallocate) and translates them into set-based database transactions, executing multi-gigabyte operations in sub-millisecond time.

docs.title: Explanation: Performance Optimization Pipeline
docs.text:
Feature: spec.optimize.OptimizationRoadmap

pgfs incorporates a structured performance optimization pipeline targeting database access latency, connection concurrency, userspace buffering, and FUSE kernel-transport tuning.

OptimizationRoadmap addresses bottlenecks across all layers of the filesystem stack: database schema design (integer inode keys, chunked block storage), transaction latency (batching, WAL tuning), memory management (page-aligned dirty write buffering), and kernel VFS interaction (attribute TTL caching, writeback cache coalescing). Together, these optimizations deliver near-native filesystem throughput.

docs.title: Explanation: Reliable Mount & Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.ReliableMount

The filesystem mounts and unmounts cleanly. Crashing or killing the daemon never leaves a ghost mount behind.

ReliableMount combines FUSE AutoUnmount kernel flags with dedicated signal handling threads to guarantee that process exits, panics, or external termination signals always trigger a clean kernel unmount, preventing dangling mount points and stale state.

docs.title: Explanation: Replicated Physical Standby Storage
docs.text:
Feature: spec.replica.ReplicatedFilesystem

A pgfs mount can be backed by a primary Postgres and a physical streaming standby in Docker. Writes go to the primary; reads are served from whichever node is authoritative at that instant, falling back to the primary when the standby lags. The filesystem is eventually consistent with the standby's lag continuously bounded by the freshness check, and a standby failure never causes data loss or a kernel-visible error.

ReplicatedFilesystem offloads read traffic to physical streaming standby replicas while preserving strict POSIX consistency. All mutating file operations execute synchronously on the primary database node. Read operations query the standby only when its WAL replay LSN confirms it is synchronized with the primary. If replication lag exceeds tolerance or the replica fails, reads immediately and silently fall back to the primary, guaranteeing data consistency and zero application downtime.

docs.title: How-To: Atomic Renames & Lock-Move Semantics
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.AtomicRename

Users can rename (move) files and directories with standard mv semantics, including overwriting existing files and empty directories.

To rename entries safely on pgfs: - Use standard mv <src> <dst> or rename(oldpath, newpath) syscall. - If replacing an existing target, ensure target is a file or empty directory. - Lock-and-rename atomic patterns (such as those used by git init and compilers) are supported out-of-the-box.

docs.title: How-To: Dual-Interface Storage Architecture
docs.text:
Feature: spec.optimize.DualInterfaceArchitecture

pgfs features a Dual-Interface Storage Architecture providing a sub-100µs Local In-Process Engine (pgrx + zero SQL parsing + io_uring zero copy) and a scalable Remote Async Network Engine (tokio-postgres + pipelining).

To configure storage backends in pgfs: - For single-node maximum performance, use --backend local to connect via shared-memory ring buffers (shm_mq) to the pgrx background worker. - For networked or distributed setups, use --backend remote to connect via tokio-postgres TCP connection pools (bb8). - To configure connection pool concurrency for remote backend, pass --max-pool-size <N>.

docs.title: How-To: POSIX Flat Filesystem
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.FlatFilesystem

Users can create, read, write, and delete files through standard POSIX file operations on the mounted directory.

To manage regular files on a mounted pgfs volume: - To create an empty file or open with creation flags, use touch <path> or standard open(path, O_CREAT). - To write arbitrary byte sequences, invoke standard POSIX write() or redirect output stream to the file path. - To read file contents, open the path with O_RDONLY and issue read() calls. - To remove a file, call unlink(path) or use rm <path>.

docs.title: How-To: Hierarchical Directory Trees
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.HierarchicalDirectories

Users can create nested directories, list their contents, and remove empty directories through standard POSIX directory operations.

To work with hierarchical directories in pgfs: - To create nested directories, run mkdir -p <dir_path>. - To list directory contents, call readdir via ls or standard directory stream APIs. - To remove a directory, ensure all children are deleted first, then invoke rmdir <dir_path>.

docs.title: How-To: Database-Native Kernel Acceleration
docs.text:
Feature: spec.offload.KernelOffloadingAcceleration

pgfs incorporates Database-Native Kernel Offloading capabilities, utilizing copy_file_range, fallocate, reflink CoW, and server-side search to eliminate userspace byte streaming and deliver sub-millisecond execution for large-scale file operations.

To leverage database-native kernel offloading: - Use standard copy_file_range(2) or cp --reflink=always for zero-copy file duplication. - Use fallocate(fd, FALLOC_FL_PUNCH_HOLE | FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE, offset, len) to deallocate block ranges. - Execute content searches via GIN/trigram index queries rather than scanning entire files across FUSE.

docs.title: How-To: Performance Optimization Pipeline
docs.text:
Feature: spec.optimize.OptimizationRoadmap

pgfs incorporates a structured performance optimization pipeline targeting database access latency, connection concurrency, userspace buffering, and FUSE kernel-transport tuning.

To tune pgfs performance for high IOPS workloads: - Enable 64KB/128KB chunked block storage (blocks(ino, block_no, data)) to prevent full-file blob rewrites. - Use prepared SQL statements (PreparedStatementReq) to eliminate query parsing overhead on hot paths. - Enable synchronous commit tuning (SET synchronous_commit = off) to reduce WAL fsync wait times. - Set --attr-ttl <seconds> to cache inode attributes in Linux VFS and avoid repetitive getattr round-trips.

docs.title: How-To: Reliable Mount & Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.ReliableMount

The filesystem mounts and unmounts cleanly. Crashing or killing the daemon never leaves a ghost mount behind.

To ensure reliable mounting and clean shutdown: - Mount with AutoUnmount flag enabled in FUSE session options. - Use SIGINT, SIGTERM, or SIGHUP to trigger explicit graceful unmount. - Poll /tmp/pgfs-*.ready to check daemon readiness before performing file I/O.

docs.title: How-To: Replicated Physical Standby Storage
docs.text:
Feature: spec.replica.ReplicatedFilesystem

A pgfs mount can be backed by a primary Postgres and a physical streaming standby in Docker. Writes go to the primary; reads are served from whichever node is authoritative at that instant, falling back to the primary when the standby lags. The filesystem is eventually consistent with the standby's lag continuously bounded by the freshness check, and a standby failure never causes data loss or a kernel-visible error.

To deploy and operate replicated pgfs: - Pass --replica <connstring> to specify the standby PostgreSQL database connection. - Ensure the primary PostgreSQL daemon listens on TCP loopback (-h 127.0.0.1) and accepts replication connections in pg_hba.conf. - Inspect daemon log lines or REPLICA_READ_COUNT and REPLICA_FALLBACK_COUNT metrics to verify read-routing health.

docs.title: Reference: Atomic Renames & Lock-Move Semantics
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.AtomicRename

Users can rename (move) files and directories with standard mv semantics, including overwriting existing files and empty directories.

AtomicRename Semantics & Error Matrix: - rename(old_parent, old_name, new_parent, new_name): Atomic move in single SQL transaction. - Target exists file -> atomically replaced. - Target exists empty directory -> atomically replaced. - Target exists non-empty directory -> ENOTEMPTY. - Source file & target directory -> EISDIR; Source directory & target file -> ENOTDIR. - Renaming directory updates parent pointers of all descendants in transaction.

docs.title: Reference: Dual-Interface Storage Architecture
docs.text:
Feature: spec.optimize.DualInterfaceArchitecture

pgfs features a Dual-Interface Storage Architecture providing a sub-100µs Local In-Process Engine (pgrx + zero SQL parsing + io_uring zero copy) and a scalable Remote Async Network Engine (tokio-postgres + pipelining).

DualInterfaceArchitecture Component Reference: - PgfsBackendTraitReq: Unified async trait specifying storage engine methods (lookup, read_block, write_block, etc.). - LocalPgrxEngineReq: Runs inside PostgreSQL via pgrx postmaster background worker (pg_bgworker), pre-compiling SPI plans (SPIPlanPtr) and processing binary Datum values. - IoUringBufferRingReq: Uses Linux 6.9+ fuse-io_uring SQ/CQ rings with pre-registered buffer rings for zero-copy VFS payloads. - RemoteAsyncBackendReq: Uses fuse3 async FUSE bindings with tokio-postgres connection pools (bb8) over TCP/Unix sockets.

docs.title: Reference: POSIX Flat Filesystem
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.FlatFilesystem

Users can create, read, write, and delete files through standard POSIX file operations on the mounted directory.

FlatFilesystem Interface & Callbacks: - create(parent_ino, name, mode, flags) -> (ino, attr): Inserts entry with kind='file', size=0. - read(ino, offset, size) -> bytes: Returns byte slice clamped to stored blob length. - write(ino, offset, data) -> bytes_written: Updates or extends byte blob in PostgreSQL. - unlink(parent_ino, name) -> status: Removes row from database and inode map. - Error codes: ENOENT (file missing), EEXIST (creation conflict), EIO (database failure).

docs.title: Reference: Hierarchical Directory Trees
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.HierarchicalDirectories

Users can create nested directories, list their contents, and remove empty directories through standard POSIX directory operations.

HierarchicalDirectories Callbacks & Rules: - mkdir(parent_ino, name, mode) -> (ino, attr): Inserts dir entry with nlink=2, permissions 0755. - rmdir(parent_ino, name) -> status: Deletes dir row if child count == 0; else replies ENOTEMPTY. - readdir(ino, offset) -> entries: Synthesizes '.' and '..' then yields child inodes. - Root directory fixed inode: ino = 1.

docs.title: Reference: Database-Native Kernel Acceleration
docs.text:
Feature: spec.offload.KernelOffloadingAcceleration

pgfs incorporates Database-Native Kernel Offloading capabilities, utilizing copy_file_range, fallocate, reflink CoW, and server-side search to eliminate userspace byte streaming and deliver sub-millisecond execution for large-scale file operations.

KernelOffloadingAcceleration Callbacks & Requirements: - CopyFileRangeReq: Executes INSERT INTO blocks SELECT ... inside PostgreSQL. - FallocatePunchHoleReq: Deletes block rows DELETE FROM blocks WHERE ino = $1 AND block_no BETWEEN $2 AND $3. - ReflinkBlockSharingReq: Reference-counted Copy-on-Write (ref_count increment on reflink, lazy copy on write). - CloneSubtreeReq: Recursive single-transaction set-based subtree copy (INSERT INTO entries SELECT ...). - ContentSearchOffloadReq: PostgreSQL GIN & pg_trgm index search pushdown.

docs.title: Reference: Performance Optimization Pipeline
docs.text:
Feature: spec.optimize.OptimizationRoadmap

pgfs incorporates a structured performance optimization pipeline targeting database access latency, connection concurrency, userspace buffering, and FUSE kernel-transport tuning.

OptimizationRoadmap Requirements & Parameters: - Schema: Chunked block storage (ChunkedBlockStorageReq) + integer inode primary keys (InoBasedRekeyingReq). - Database Tuning: PreparedStatementReq, TransactionBatchingReq, SynchronousCommitTuningReq, UnloggedTableOptReq. - Transport Tuning: KernelAttrCacheTtlReq (--attr-ttl), KernelWritebackCacheReq (FUSE_WRITEBACK_CACHE), BufferedWriteFlushReq. - Sparse Data Safety: SparseWritePaddingReq (pre-zero padding on uninstantiated block writes).

docs.title: Reference: Reliable Mount & Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.ReliableMount

The filesystem mounts and unmounts cleanly. Crashing or killing the daemon never leaves a ghost mount behind.

ReliableMount Lifecycle Specification: - Mount flags: AutoUnmount enabled. - Signal management: Dedicated sigwait thread handles SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP. - Control files: /tmp/pgfs-{hash}.pid (daemon PID), /tmp/pgfs-{hash}.ready (readiness marker). - Panic recovery: panic = "abort" in release builds ensures instant exit and kernel mount cleanup.

docs.title: Reference: Replicated Physical Standby Storage
docs.text:
Feature: spec.replica.ReplicatedFilesystem

A pgfs mount can be backed by a primary Postgres and a physical streaming standby in Docker. Writes go to the primary; reads are served from whichever node is authoritative at that instant, falling back to the primary when the standby lags. The filesystem is eventually consistent with the standby's lag continuously bounded by the freshness check, and a standby failure never causes data loss or a kernel-visible error.

ReplicatedFilesystem Specifications & Requirements: - Provisioning: StartsDockerStandby (scripts/replica_db.sh), RequiresPrimaryTcpListener. - Connection & Routing: AcceptsReplicaConnection (--replica), ServesReadsFromReplica (getattr, readdir, read), WritesStayOnPrimary (mutations on primary). - Consistency: DetectsReplicationLag (checks LSN replay lag pg_last_wal_replay_lsn), FallsBackToPrimary (transparent fallback on lag/error). - Observability: ReplicaObservability (REPLICA_READ_COUNT, REPLICA_FALLBACK_COUNT, SIGUSR1 status dump).

docs.title: Tutorial: Atomic Renames & Lock-Move Semantics
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.AtomicRename

Users can rename (move) files and directories with standard mv semantics, including overwriting existing files and empty directories.

In this tutorial, we will perform atomic file and directory renames. 1. Create a source file: echo 'v1' > ./mnt/a.txt and target file echo 'v2' > ./mnt/b.txt. 2. Execute mv ./mnt/a.txt ./mnt/b.txt to atomically replace b.txt with a.txt. 3. Verify ./mnt/b.txt contains 'v1' and ./mnt/a.txt no longer exists. 4. Test directory subtree rename: mkdir ./mnt/old_dir and move it with mv ./mnt/old_dir ./mnt/new_dir.

docs.title: Tutorial: Dual-Interface Storage Architecture
docs.text:
Feature: spec.optimize.DualInterfaceArchitecture

pgfs features a Dual-Interface Storage Architecture providing a sub-100µs Local In-Process Engine (pgrx + zero SQL parsing + io_uring zero copy) and a scalable Remote Async Network Engine (tokio-postgres + pipelining).

In this tutorial, we will explore selecting between local in-process and remote network backends. 1. Launch pgfs with the remote async engine: ./target/release/pgfs --backend remote --conn postgres://.... 2. Benchmark read/write latency using make test-integration or custom fio workloads. 3. Build the local pgrx extension and start PostgreSQL postmaster with the pgrx worker enabled. 4. Launch pgfs with the local engine: ./target/release/pgfs --backend local --shm /dev/shm/pgfs. 5. Compare latency metrics to observe sub-100µs file operation latencies.

docs.title: Tutorial: POSIX Flat Filesystem
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.FlatFilesystem

Users can create, read, write, and delete files through standard POSIX file operations on the mounted directory.

In this tutorial, we will mount a pgfs filesystem and perform basic POSIX file operations. 1. Start the pgfs daemon mounted at ./mnt. 2. Create a file using echo 'Hello pgfs' > ./mnt/demo.txt. 3. Read the file back with cat ./mnt/demo.txt and verify the content. 4. Append data using echo 'More content' >> ./mnt/demo.txt. 5. Delete the file using rm ./mnt/demo.txt and confirm it no longer appears in ls ./mnt.

docs.title: Tutorial: Hierarchical Directory Trees
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.HierarchicalDirectories

Users can create nested directories, list their contents, and remove empty directories through standard POSIX directory operations.

In this tutorial, we will work with directory trees in pgfs. 1. Create a nested directory structure: mkdir -p ./mnt/docs/project/src. 2. List directory contents with ls -la ./mnt/docs/project to see '.' and '..' entries. 3. Create files inside nested subdirectories: touch ./mnt/docs/project/src/main.rs. 4. Try removing a non-empty directory with rmdir ./mnt/docs/project and observe the ENOTEMPTY error. 5. Delete sub-files first, then remove empty directories using rmdir ./mnt/docs/project/src.

docs.title: Tutorial: Database-Native Kernel Acceleration
docs.text:
Feature: spec.offload.KernelOffloadingAcceleration

pgfs incorporates Database-Native Kernel Offloading capabilities, utilizing copy_file_range, fallocate, reflink CoW, and server-side search to eliminate userspace byte streaming and deliver sub-millisecond execution for large-scale file operations.

In this tutorial, we will use kernel offloading features in pgfs to clone files and directories instantly. 1. Create a large source file: head -c 100M /dev/urandom > ./mnt/large.bin. 2. Perform an instant copy using cp --reflink=always ./mnt/large.bin ./mnt/clone.bin. 3. Notice that the copy completes instantaneously (<5ms) because PostgreSQL copied block reference IDs. 4. Punch a sparse hole using fallocate -p -o 1M -l 10M ./mnt/clone.bin. 5. Verify hole punching freed space in PostgreSQL without re-writing the rest of the file.

docs.title: Tutorial: Performance Optimization Pipeline
docs.text:
Feature: spec.optimize.OptimizationRoadmap

pgfs incorporates a structured performance optimization pipeline targeting database access latency, connection concurrency, userspace buffering, and FUSE kernel-transport tuning.

In this tutorial, we will apply and benchmark key pgfs performance tuning options. 1. Start pgfs with kernel attribute caching enabled: ./target/release/pgfs --attr-ttl 5.0. 2. Enable writeback caching in kernel VFS: ./target/release/pgfs --writeback-cache. 3. Run scripts/bench_profile.sh to measure throughput across small-block write and read phases. 4. Observe latency histogram metrics printed in daemon logs to evaluate p50, p95, and p99 performance.

docs.title: Tutorial: Reliable Mount & Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
Feature: spec.app.ReliableMount

The filesystem mounts and unmounts cleanly. Crashing or killing the daemon never leaves a ghost mount behind.

In this tutorial, we will verify clean daemon mount and shutdown behavior. 1. Mount pgfs using scripts/pgfs.sh up. 2. Verify mount point status via scripts/pgfs.sh status and check PID file at /tmp/pgfs-*.pid. 3. Send SIGINT to the daemon process or run scripts/pgfs.sh down. 4. Verify the mountpoint is cleanly unmounted and no stale daemon processes remain.

docs.title: Tutorial: Replicated Physical Standby Storage
docs.text:
Feature: spec.replica.ReplicatedFilesystem

A pgfs mount can be backed by a primary Postgres and a physical streaming standby in Docker. Writes go to the primary; reads are served from whichever node is authoritative at that instant, falling back to the primary when the standby lags. The filesystem is eventually consistent with the standby's lag continuously bounded by the freshness check, and a standby failure never causes data loss or a kernel-visible error.

In this tutorial, we will set up and verify a replicated pgfs mount with primary/standby PostgreSQL. 1. Start the Docker streaming standby container: ./scripts/replica_db.sh up. 2. Launch pgfs with primary and standby parameters: ./target/release/pgfs --conn postgres://127.0.0.1:5432/pgfs --replica postgres://127.0.0.1:5433/pgfs. 3. Perform write operations (touch ./mnt/data.txt) and observe writes directed to primary. 4. Perform read operations (cat ./mnt/data.txt) and observe reads served from the standby node. 5. Stop the standby container (./scripts/replica_db.sh down) and verify reads seamlessly fall back to primary without errors.
